text:
Usually, no—Monzo’s paid plans are only worth it if you will genuinely use the specific benefits. For most UK users, the free Monzo account is already strong; Extra is the easiest small upgrade, Perks can pay for itself if you use several lifestyle perks, and Max is mainly a bundled-insurance decision.
monzo

Current plans and prices
Plan	Monthly cost	Best for	Main extras
Free	£0	Most people	Full current account, budgeting, Pots, 2.80% AER instant-access savings, one connected account, one virtual card. 
monzo

Extra	£3	People who want better money management	Unlimited connected accounts, up to five virtual cards, advanced round-ups, custom categories, two credit scores, 3.15% AER instant-access savings. 
monzo

Perks	£9	Regular rail users and people who will use the partner offers	Annual Railcard, weekly Greggs treat, monthly Vue ticket, Uber One, YouTube Premium Lite, 3.55% AER instant-access savings, £600 monthly overseas ATM allowance. 
monzo

Max	From £19	People who would otherwise buy travel, phone and breakdown cover	Everything in Perks plus worldwide travel insurance, worldwide phone insurance, UK/Europe breakdown cover, and 3.80% AER instant-access savings; family cover costs an extra £4. 
monzo

How to judge value

The key question is not “are the perks worth £300 a year?” but “would I buy or use these things anyway?” Monzo itself values Perks’ partner benefits at over £300 a year, but that is only real value if you would otherwise pay for them or would use them regularly.
monzo

Extra (£36/year): Worth it if you value connected accounts, virtual cards, custom budgeting, or a higher savings rate. It is the least risky paid upgrade because the features are broadly useful rather than dependent on lifestyle habits.
monzo

Perks (£108/year): Potentially good value if you travel by train, use Uber Eats/Uber, watch YouTube, and would claim the Greggs and Vue benefits. If you would use only the Railcard, it is unlikely to justify £9 a month on its own.
monzo

Max (£228/year, or £276 with family): Worth considering only if you do not already have equivalent cover and would otherwise buy annual travel insurance, phone insurance, and breakdown cover. Check eligibility, excesses, claim limits, and exclusions first—particularly age limits, pre-existing medical conditions, phone value, and the insurance provider’s terms.
monzo

Savings-rate caveat

The higher savings rates are a real benefit, but not automatically enough to cover the subscription. Moving from the free plan’s 2.80% AER to Max’s 3.80% AER is a 1 percentage-point uplift; on £10,000, that is about £100 a year before tax considerations—well below Max’s £228 annual cost.
monzo

You would need roughly £22,800 in the relevant instant-access savings Pot for that 1-point uplift alone to offset Max’s annual fee. And Monzo’s rates are variable, so they can change.
monzo

My practical recommendation

Choose Free if you mainly want a well-designed UK current account, spending insights, Pots, and ordinary overseas card spending.

Choose Extra if you actively budget across several banks or value virtual cards; it is the most defensible upgrade at £3 a month.
monzo

Choose Perks only after listing the perks you will actually claim each month; it works best for a regular commuter who also uses several of the partner benefits.
monzo

Choose Max only if the insurance bundle replaces cover you would otherwise buy, and you are comfortable with the policy terms. Otherwise, buying only the insurance you need is likely better value.
monzo

One important distinction: Monzo’s paid plans are packaged bank accounts, not an essential banking upgrade. The free account still includes FSCS protection for eligible deposits up to £120,000 per person, so you are not paying for core account safety.
monzo
